faq.a: Yes, if the patient is haemodynamically stable, β‑hCG <5000 IU/L, ectopic ≤3 cm and no contraindications to methotrexate.
faq.q: Can a small ectopic be managed medically in a low‑resource hospital?

faq.a: MVA uses a soft suction cup, reduces uterine trauma, needs less anaesthesia and has lower infection rates.
faq.q: Why is manual vacuum aspiration preferred over sharp curettage?

faq.a: Activate emergency response, give IV crystalloids, cross‑match blood, and arrange immediate surgical intervention.
faq.q: What is the first step if a patient with suspected ruptured ectopic is unstable?

exam: A 24‑year‑old presents with sudden left lower‑quadrant pain, shoulder tip pain and a BP of 85/50 mmHg. What is your immediate management? — Recognise ruptured ectopic, give IV fluids, type‑and‑cross, prepare for emergency salpingectomy.

β‑hCG is 3500 IU/L and ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a 2 cm adnexal mass. Which treatment is appropriate and why? — Single‑dose methotrexate; stable, small ectopic, preserves fertility, avoids surgery.

A patient with threatened miscarriage has a closed cervix and mild spotting. What advice do you give regarding activity? — Recommend pelvic rest, avoid heavy lifting and intercourse for 1 week, reassure that most continue to term.

After manual vacuum aspiration, the patient develops fever and lower‑abdominal tenderness. What is the most likely complication and next step? — Post‑abortion sepsis; start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics and obtain blood cultures.
How does the β‑hCG rise pattern help differentiate a viable intra‑uterine pregnancy from an ectopic? — Viable pregnancy doubles every 48 h; ectopic shows plateau or suboptimal rise.
In a setting without ultrasound, what clinical signs point toward a ruptured ectopic? — Unilateral pain, shoulder tip pain, peritoneal irritation, hypotension, and a positive pregnancy test.
Why is methotrexate contraindicated in a patient with active pulmonary TB? — Methotrexate is immunosuppressive and can worsen TB, increasing morbidity.
What contraception should be offered after treatment of an ectopic pregnancy and why? — Long‑acting reversible methods (IUD or implant) to reduce repeat ectopic risk and ensure spacing.
ai.title: First Trimester Pregnancy Complications
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Covers the common urgent problems seen at the end of the first trimester in low‑resource settings – ectopic pregnancy, threatened miscarriage and incomplete abortion – with a bedside, investigative and management focus.

b: Ectopic pregnancy: gestational sac outside the uterine cavity.
Threatened miscarriage: vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix and viable intra‑uterine pregnancy.
Incomplete abortion: passage of products of conception with an open cervix and retained tissue.
sections.p: Any pregnancy‑related problem occurring between 10 and 14 weeks gestation that threatens maternal health or fetal viability.

b: Stable: normal BP, HR <100, no peritoneal signs.
Unstable: SBP <90 mmHg, HR ≥100, abdominal guarding or rebound.
Ectopic stage I: unruptured, ≤3 cm, no haemoperitoneum.
Ectopic stage II: ruptured or >3 cm with haemoperitoneum.
sections.p: Severity is graded by haemodynamic status and gestational sac location.

b: Ectopic: prior tubal surgery, PID (often from untreated chlamydia), tubal damage from schistosomiasis, assisted conception.
Threatened miscarriage: uterine anomalies, infection (malaria, TB), smoking, poor nutrition.
Incomplete abortion: unsafe self‑induced abortion, herbal remedies, infection.
sections.p: Risk factors differ by condition but overlap in low‑resource settings.

b: Sudden unilateral lower‑abdominal pain, shoulder tip pain, faintness → ruptured ectopic.
Vaginal spotting or heavy bleeding, crampy lower‑abdominal pain, closed cervix → threatened miscarriage.
Bleeding with tissue passage, open cervix, uterine size smaller than dates → incomplete abortion.
sections.p: History and exam guide the differential.

t.b: Is there an intra‑uterine gestational sac? → Presence confirms viable pregnancy; absence with adnexal mass suggests ectopic.
Is the rise appropriate for gestational age? → Doubling every 48 h is normal; plateau or decline suggests ectopic or failing pregnancy.
Is the patient anaemic or haemodynamically compromised? → Low Hb/Hct signals significant blood loss; if unavailable, use clinical signs of shock.
Is there concurrent urinary tract infection? → Positive nitrites/leukocytes guide antibiotic choice when infection is suspected.

b: Ruptured ectopic: sudden hypotension, tachycardia, shoulder tip pain, peritoneal signs.
Sepsis: fever, foul‑smelling discharge, tachycardia after abortion.
Ectopic (unstable or large): laparoscopic or open salpingectomy – definitive control of haemorrhage.
Threatened miscarriage: expectant management, pelvic rest, anti‑emetics; give oral iron if anaemic.
Incomplete abortion: manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) – safe, low‑resource; give broad‑spectrum antibiotic (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) if infection risk.
All patients: give tetanus prophylaxis, counsel on contraception, screen for HIV/TB where endemic.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, stabilise the patient and prevent recurrence.

b: β‑hCG repeat 1 week after treatment to confirm decline to <5 IU/L.
Ultrasound 2 weeks later to confirm empty uterus or resolved ectopic.
Counselling on safe abortion methods, STI prevention, and early antenatal booking.
sections.p: Ensure resolution and address future pregnancy safety.

b: Appendicitis – right lower‑quadrant pain without pregnancy signs; ultrasound helps differentiate.
Ovarian torsion – acute pain, adnexal mass; Doppler flow assessment.
Urinary tract infection – dysuria, flank pain; urine dipstick distinguishes.
β‑hCG plateau may occur in normal early pregnancy if drawn too early; repeat after 48 h.
Ultrasound may miss a small ectopic if the operator is inexperienced; consider repeat scan or laparoscopy if suspicion remains.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with fainting or low blood pressure
Fever >38 °C with abdominal pain after abortion
